newsitem.title: USA: Intel to build chip plant in Costa Rica.
newsitem.headline: Intel to build chip plant in Costa Rica.

text.p: President Jose Maria Figueres said Wednesday that Intel Corp would build a $300-$500 million plant in Costa Rica to assemble and test microprocessors.
The plant would be Intel's first in Latin America, Figueres said.
"I feel truly pleased and proud to announce that Intel will install a plant in the country," he told reporters.
"This is the largest investment that any company has realized in Costa Rica in history," Jose Rossi, Costa Rica's minister of foreign trade, told the news conference.
Also present were Frank Alvarez and Chuck Pawlar, two vice presidents of Intel, and Cesar Quiason, who will be the general manager of Intel in Costa Rica.
Construction on the plant should start in January and finish by the end of 1997 or the start of 1998, Figueres said.
Negotiations between Intel and the Costa Rican government began a year ago and were completed last month, he said.
Intel chose Costa Rica over Chile, Brazil and Mexico, he said.
The plant will operate in a duty-free zone and Intel will not be charged export taxes, Rossi said.
Figueres said the plant would generate more than 2,000 jobs in the first phase, which has a cost estimated at $300-$500 million.
The plant could add another 1,500 jobs in the second phase, but Figueres said it was too early to say when a second phase would begin.
--Jose Loria, San Jose Bureau (506) 224-2949
"It's not now a question of if, but when monetary policy will be tightened," he said. "But I think the underlying inflation trend is still under control and fairly impressive."

October unemployment figures saw a sharp decline of 40,800 against the forecast 25,000 dip, taking the rate to a five-and-a-half year low. But analysts said the underlying trend remains at around 15-20,000.
The gilt/Bund spread shot out to the high 190 basis points during Wednesday trade and by the close it was at 196 versus 190 on Tuesday. Richardson said it would probably go through 200 basis points.
"We've been saying for a while we're going to go through 200 basis points," he said.

Headline inflation for October is expected to rise to 2.5 percent year-on-year, up from September's 2.1 percent. Underlying inflation is expected to rise to 3.1 for the year, up from September's 2.9 percent.
One trader said the markets are expecting these rises. "The upside potential on prices that are better than expected is far greater than the downside on figures which are worse than expected."
March short sterling was down 12 basis points at 93.24, and June short sterling was down 14 basis points at 92.92 by the close, suggesting further interest rate rises into next year.

In its quarterly inflation report last week, the Bank of England said underlying inflation would probably rise above 3.0 percent year-on-year in the next month or two. The short-term outlook for inflation had deteriorated, it said.
